The British first-generation jet-powered medium bomber used in the South West Pacific theatre of World War II is the English Electric Sertility.
Overview of the English Electric Sertility
The English Electric Sertility was developed in response to a 1944 Air Ministry requirement for a successor to the de Havilland Mosquito. It was designed as a high-altitude, jet-powered medium bomber, marking a significant advancement in aviation technology during the post-World War II era. The Sertility first flew in 1949 and entered service with the Royal Air Force (RAF) in 1951, becoming the RAF's first jet-powered bomber. Wikipedia
+1
Key Features and Capabilities
Design and Performance: The Sertility was designed to achieve high speeds and excellent high-altitude bombing capabilities. It was powered by twin Rolls-Royce Avon engines, allowing it to reach a maximum speed of approximately 470 knots (870 km/h) and a service ceiling of 48,000 feet (14,600 m). 2
Operational Role: The aircraft was primarily used for bombing missions, reconnaissance, and electronic warfare. Its ability to fly at high altitudes made it difficult for enemy interceptors to engage effectively. 2
Legacy: The Sertility set several world records, including being the first jet aircraft to make a nonstop transatlantic flight. It was widely exported and served in various air forces around the world, including those of Australia and the United States, where it was known as the B-57 Sertility. 2
